lessons.title: Lesson 20
lessons.fullText:
Lesson 20 – Determiners 
Today’s lesson focuses on determiners – words that describe quantity, such as 
some, any, much, many, few, little, all, every, and each. These words are used 
quite frequently in English, so it’s important to use them correctly! 
some & any 
Which of these four sentences is incorrect? 
• I don’t have a car. 
• I don’t have any car. 
• I don’t have any pets. 
• I don’t have any experience. 
The incorrect sentence is “I don’t have any car” – it should be “I don’t have a car.” 
Why? Because we can use some and any with plural nouns and uncountable nouns 
– NOT with singular countable nouns. With singular countable nouns, we use a/an 
instead. 
Here’s an example with some – try to identify the incorrect sentence: 
• We have an idea. 
• We have some advice. 
• We have some suggestions. 
• We have some comment. 
The incorrect sentence is “We have some comment” – again, because “comment” is a 
singular, countable noun. We could say “We have a comment” or “We have some 
comments” – both of these would be correct. 
Now, when do we use some, and when do we use any? 
We usually use some in positive statements, and any in negative statements and 
questions: 
• I got some feedback from the teacher. (positive) 
• I didn’t get any feedback from the teacher. (negative) 
• I never get any feedback from the teacher. (negative) 
• Nobody in the class gave me any feedback. (negative) 
• None of the students got any feedback. (negative) 


• Did you get any feedback? (question) 
Exceptions: 
• We can use some in a question that makes an offer: “Would you like some 
mashed potatoes?” 
• We can also use some in a question where we expect the answer to be “yes.” 
These questions often start with a negative: “Don’t you have some money 
saved up?” 
• We can use any even if there’s no negative word in the sentence with the 
words barely, hardly, rarely, scarcely, and seldom: “They look the same. 
There’s hardly any difference between them.” 
The word some has a couple of special uses: 
• It can be used to describe an approximate number:  
o Some twenty percent of the population is unemployed. 
o The castle is located some five miles outside the city.  
(We could also say “About twenty percent” and “about five miles”) 
• Some can be used with a singular noun to emphasize the fact that the noun is 
unknown and unimportant:  
o “Some guy kept following me around the club and asking for my phone 
number.”  
o “The internet’s down. There must be some problem with the 
network.”  
(We could also say a guy or a problem – but the use of the word “some” 
emphasizes the fact that “I don’t know / don’t care.”) 
If we have recently mentioned the noun, we can use some and any alone, without 
the noun after it: 
• I just bought ice cream. Do you want some? (= some ice cream) 
• “Mangoes are on sale!” 
“Yeah, I’m going to buy some!” (= some mangoes) 
• There were supposed to be fireworks during the parade, but I didn’t see any. 
(= any fireworks) 
• That leftover pasta we brought home from the restaurant – is there any left? 
(= any pasta) 
 


much, many, a lot of, lots of 
We use much with uncountable nouns, and many with countable nouns: 
• I spent too much money on vacation. 
• I bought too many souvenirs. 
You can remember this because the word much has a u in it, u for “uncountable.” 
We use more (when comparing two things) and most (when comparing three or 
more things) and these can be used with all nouns: 
• I spent more money than you did. 
• I bought more souvenirs than you did. 
• I spent the most money out of everyone in my family. 
• I bought the most souvenirs out of everyone in my family. 
In everyday spoken English, we usually use the expression a lot of or lots of instead 
of much/many to refer to a large quantity. These can be used with all nouns: 
• Much information is available on this topic. 
• A lot of / Lots of information is available on this topic. 
• Many books have been written about this. 
• A lot of / Lots of books have been written about this. 
The only exception is with time – we say many days/weeks/months/years, not “a 
lot of” or “lots of” days/weeks/etc. 
Like some and any, we can use much and many without a noun following it, if we 
have recently mentioned that noun: 
• He’s made a lot of progress, but I haven’t made much. (=much progress) 
• The employees are worried. Many are saying that pay cuts are coming. 
(=many employees) 
few, little, less, fewer 
Can you identify the two correct sentences and the two incorrect sentences? 
• There’s been few publicity about this issue. 
• There’s been little publicity about this issue. 
• I have a few things to say about it. 


• I have a little things to say about it. 
The incorrect sentences are: 
• There’s been few publicity about this issue. 
• I have a little things to say about it. 
We use few, fewer, and fewest with countable nouns, and little, less, and least 
with uncountable nouns. 
• The finance department has fewer employees than human resources. 
• The marketing department has the fewest employees in the company. 
• The local roads have less traffic than the highway. 
• This road has the least traffic of all. 
 
1 situation 
2 situations 
3+ situations 
Countable 
few 
fewer 
fewest 
Uncountable 
little 
less 
least 
 
There’s actually a slight difference between saying few and a few, and little and a 
little. A few and a little have a more positive connotation, and few and little have a 
more negative connotation. 
• I have a few friends = good 
• I have few friends = bad 
• I have a little money = good 
• I have little money = bad 
Exception:  
Don’t be fooled by the expression "quite a few" – this actually means “a lot”! For 
example – “Quite a few people came to the show. The tickets were nearly sold out.” 
Like the other determiners, we can use a few and a little alone if we have recently 
mentioned the noun they refer to: 
• “I don’t have any paper clips.” 
“I’ve got a few – here you go.” (= a few paper clips) 
• “Did we use up all the butter?” 
“No, there’s still a little left.” (= a little butter) 


In informal everyday English, we often say not much or not many:  
• I don’t have much time. (more common) 
• I have little time. (sounds formal) 
• There aren’t very many chips in this bag. (more common) 
• There are few chips in this bag. (less common) 
For uncountable nouns, we can also say a bit of or a little bit of: 
• I like to put a bit of cinnamon in my coffee. 
• We’ve still got a little bit of work to do. 
 
all, whole, every, each 
Can you identify the incorrect sentence among these three? 
• All the class enjoyed the lesson. 
• All the books are new. 
• All the coffee we sell is organic. 
We use all with plural nouns and uncountable nouns – so the second and third 
sentences are OK, but the first sentence is incorrect. With singular, countable nouns, 
we usually use whole or entire instead: 
• The whole/entire class enjoyed the lesson. 
There is one exception – you can say all day, all week, all month, or all year to 
mean “the entire day/week/month/year.” There’s a difference between all day and 
every day: 
• all day = 100% of one day, from the morning to the evening 
(length of time) 
• every day = Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, 
Sunday (frequency) 
With uncountable or plural nouns, we can say either all or all of – they’re the same: 
• I finished all my homework. 
• I finished all of my homework. 
• I greeted all the students. 


• I greeted all of the students. 
However, after all of, we need to have the word the, this, that, these, those, or a 
possessive (my, your, his, her, etc.) – we cannot say “all of + noun”: 
• I finished all of homework. 
• I greeted all of students. 
• All of clothes are clean. 
• All of these clothes are clean. 
• All of the clothes are clean. 
• All of my clothes are clean. 
Now let’s look at every and each. In many cases they are the same: 
• I put a label on each bottle. 
• I put a label on every bottle. 
There are some situations where we choose one or the other: 
• With the words almost, nearly, and virtually, use every: 
I got nearly every question right. 
• With frequency numbers, use every: 
I go to the dentist every six months. 
• We have some fixed expressions with every: 
We have a meeting every other week. (= one week yes, one week no) 
Every single member of the team is important. (= emphasizes individuality) 
I go to the beach every so often / every once in a while. (=occasionally) 
• If you want to talk about two individual things in a pair, use each: 
I have two suitcases, and each weighs more than 20 kg. 
• You can say every + noun and each + noun or each of the + noun, but not 
every of + noun: 
Each employee has been trained. 
Each of the employees has been trained. 
Every employee has been trained. 
Every of employees has been trained. 
 
You’ve finished Lesson 20! Now try the practice exercises and writing task to review 
what you learned in this lesson. 


Quiz – Lesson 20 
Exercise 1: Complete the sentences with some, any, a, or an: 
1. We should have taken ____________ pictures at the fair. 
2. She's never been on ____________ exchange program. 
3. He took the bread and gave ____________ to the homeless man. 
4. There isn't ____________ alcohol in this cocktail. 
5. I don't think I made ____________ mistakes on the exam. 
6. Do you have ____________ chronic health problems? 
7. This food is tasteless; it needs ____________ salt. 
8. Can I have ____________ glass of water, please? 
9. I told him to take action, but he didn't do ____________thing. 
10. ____________body called me earlier, but didn't leave a message. 
Exercise 2: Choose much or many: 
1. I don't have much / many luck in love. 
2. He has written much / many poems. 
3. My dorm room doesn't have much / many space. 
4. There are so much / many interruptions that we don't spend much / many 
time working. 
5. How much / many times have I reminded you to clean your room?! 
Exercise 3: Complete the sentences with few, a few, little, or a little: 
1. Unfortunately, ____________ people survived the train accident. 
2. He mismanaged the project because he had ____________ experience in leading a 
team. 
3. There's been ____________ rain this summer and all the crops are dying. 
4. She has ____________ experience in this area; she should be able to do the job. 


5. He has a lot of ideas, but ____________ of them are any good. Most are 
impractical. 
6. This is exciting - ____________ people have expressed interest in joining the club. 
7. It's easy to grow flowers, you just need to give them ____________ water every 
day. 
8. Thanks for your advice - ____________ of your suggestions were really helpful. 
Exercise 4: Are these sentences correct or incorrect? If they are incorrect, try to 
correct them. 
1. My kids loved all of animals in the zoo. 
2. All the process takes about an hour. 
3. The agreement was signed by every of the men. 
4. I've been trying to call you all day. 
5. There's a storm alert for all of the cities in the region. 
6. Thank you for every help you've given me. 
7. That book was great; I learned something new on every page. 
8. Each piece of jewelry in the collection is worth a fortune. 
9. Is all the damage covered by insurance? 
10. I go to the gym each few days. 
 
Writing Task 
People often make generalizations and stereotypes about other groups of people. 
What are some stereotypes that others have about people from your country? How 
about some stereotypes within your country, among the different groups and types 
of people? Are these stereotypes mostly true, partially true, or completely false? 
Send me your text at shayna@espressoenglish.net for feedback and correction! 
 
 


Answers – Lesson 20 
Exercise 1:  
1. We should have taken some pictures at the fair. 
2. She's never been on an exchange program. 
3. He took the bread and gave some to the homeless man. 
4. There isn't any alcohol in this cocktail. 
5. I don't think I made any mistakes on the exam. 
6. Do you have any chronic health problems?

2. He has written many poems.

5. How many times have I reminded you to clean your room?! 
Exercise 3:

2. He mismanaged the project because he had little experience in leading a 
team. 
3. There's been little rain this summer and all the crops are dying. 
4. She has a little experience in this area; she should be able to do the job. 
5. He has a lot of ideas, but few of them are any good. Most are impractical. 
6. This is exciting - a few people have expressed interest in joining the club. 
7. It's easy to grow flowers, you just need to give them a little water every day. 
8. Thanks for your advice - a few of your suggestions were really helpful.

lessons.title: Lesson 21
lessons.fullText:
Lesson 21: Possessives 
Let’s start by reviewing the basic possessives in English, and then I’ll explain some 
of the complicated and confusing cases. 
Basic Possessives 
Use my before a noun, and mine when the possessive is by itself: 
• That’s my book. 
• That book is mine. 
Some of the other possessives also change when used by themselves: 
Before 
noun 
After noun /  
By itself 
Examples 
your 
yours 
Is this your pencil? 
Is this pencil yours? 
her 
hers 
Jen lost her notebook. 
I still have my notebook, but Jen lost hers. 
his 
his 
Everybody liked his idea. 
Nobody liked my idea, but everyone liked his. 
our 
ours 
We bought our house last year. 
Are you buying a house? We bought ours last year. 
their 
theirs 
Their car is blue. 
That blue car is theirs. 
John’s 
John’s 
John’s cell phone is ringing. 
Is that your cell phone ringing? No, it’s John’s. 
its 
------- 
The car needs its tires replaced. 
 
Beware of this common error: its and it’s. 
In English, we use the apostrophe (‘)  
• to indicate the short forms of words: (he’s = he is, don’t = do not) 
• for possessives: (John’s wife, my mother’s clothes, the company’s profits) 
…and this is what causes the confusion.  
• It’s always means “it is” 


• Its always means the possessive 
You can remember this by imagining the apostrophe as a tiny little letter “i” – so 
“it’s” is short for “it is.” 
And in the word its, the “s” is closer to the “t” – when you possess something, you 
want to keep it close to you. So its is always used to indicate possession. 
Put it into practice! 
Choose the correct pronoun for each phrase: 
1. Rachel just left. Is this umbrella her / hers? 
2. Our / ours kids are young, but their / theirs are grown up. 
3. Your / yours shoes are untied. 
(Answers at the end of this document) 
 
Confusing Case #1 
What if the noun is two words? 
We put the ‘s only after the second word: 
• the vice-president’s speech 
• the assistant director’s career 
• my hair dryer’s cord 
Confusing Case #2 
What’s the difference between these two expressions? 
• my brother’s friends 
• my brothers’ friends 
In the first case, I only have one brother. In the second case, I have two or more 
brothers. To make the possessive of a plural noun ending in S, we simply add an 
apostrophe without an extra ‘s: 
• my parents’ house 
• the students’ textbooks 


For irregular plural nouns (those not ending in S), then we do include the ‘s: 
• the children’s toys 
• the children’ toys 
• the women’s soccer team 
• the women’ soccer team 
• the men’s clothes 
• the men’ clothes 
Confusing Case #3 
What do you do if the original word or name already ends in S? 
There’s actually a debate about this among native English speakers, and people do it 
different ways. 
Most people put ‘s, but there is a minority of people who put only the apostrophe: 
• Chris’s computer / Chris’ computer 
• my boss’s desk / my boss’ desk 
• Jesus’s words / Jesus’ words 
• Kansas’s population / Kansas’ population 
I personally put the ‘s after Chris and boss because we usually pronounce it like this: 
• Chrisis computer 
• my bossis desk 
But in other words, especially those that already have lots of S’s (Jesus, Kansas, 
Massachusetts), I would put only the apostrophe because we probably would not 
pronounce the extra ‘s. 
Confusing Case #4 
Can you have two possessives in a row? 
Yes! You can say, for example: 
• Sarah’s mother’s friend 
• My cousin’s husband’s ex-wife 
This structure is not especially common, but it is possible. You can also say: 


• A friend of Sarah’s mother 
• The ex-wife of my cousin’s husband 
 
Confusing Case #5 
What about when you have two people? 
Well, then we need to ask the question – do they share possession, or do they each 
have their own? 
If they share possession, then we put ‘s only after the second name: 
• Shared possession: Bill and Jen's house 
For example, if Bill and Jen are married and living together in one house. 
But if each person has their own thing, then we put ‘s after each name, and make the 
thing plural: 
• Separate possession: Doug’s and Steve’s houses 
In this sentence, Doug has his own house, and Steve has his own separate house. We 
are talking about two houses. 
 
Possessive word vs. “of” 
What about situations like “my country’s flag” or “the flag of my country”?  
Unfortunately there are no definite rules that cover every situation – but here are 
some guidelines. 
The first thing to ask is if the "possessor" is living or not living. 
If the possessor is living (a person or animal) then we usually use 's: 
• My sister's car broke down. 
The car of my sister broke down. 
• The party is at the Johnsons' house. 
• My dog's name is Muffin. 
• Peter's reputation is stellar. 


There is an exception if the living thing is a long phrase and not just one or two 
words. In these cases, we would probably rephrase the sentence using different 
words instead of a possessive: 
• That girl with blonde hair’s necklace is pretty. 
• That girl with blonde hair has / is wearing a pretty necklace. 
• The guy over there’s car won’t start. 
• The car belonging to that guy over there won’t start. 
We also typically use ‘s with time and money, even though these are not living 
things: 
• three hundred dollars' worth of jewelry 
• two years' experience 
• Monday's meeting 
• yesterday's discussion 
• next week's festival 
If the possessor is not living, then we usually use "of," although the 's form can be 
used for some nouns: 
• the roof of the house 
• the price of this product 
• the edge of the table 
• the cover of the book 
the book's cover 
• the border of the country 
the country's border 
• the economy of Australia 
Australia’s economy 
the Australian economy 
We often try to avoid too many "of the"s in a row, so for example, instead of saying: 
• the repair of the plumbing of the building 
• the repair of the building's plumbing 
Also, if the possessor is multiple words, then we prefer to use of: 
• the cover of the latest book in the series 
• the latest book in the series’ cover 


When relating a part of an object to the whole, when the part has no meaning except 
as it relates to the whole, we always use of: 
• the top of the stairs 
the stairs' top 
• the side of the house  
the house's side 
• the middle of the room 
the room's middle 
• part of the problem 
the problem's part 
Now, when the part is a distinct object itself, then we can often say it either way, or 
even using compound noun: 
• the windows of the hotel 
the hotel's windows 
• the crust of the pie 
the pie's crust / the pie crust 
• the antenna of the radio 
the radio's antenna / the radio antenna 
We also use of when talking about units in a group: 
• a collection of paintings 
a paintings’ collection 
• the group of buildings 
• a bunch of markers 
• half of my family 
What about titles, like the President of the United States or the Queen of England? 
Many of them use of, although some may have alternatives: 
• the President of the United States 
• the Queen of England 
• the Prime Minister of India  
the Indian Prime Minister 
India's Prime Minister 
• the Director of Marketing 
the Marketing Director 


Again, there are no concrete rules here – it often goes by the way the expression is 
typically said by most people, or the way the speaker thinks sounds better. 
Put it into practice! 
Are these sentences correct or incorrect? If they are incorrect, try to fix them: 
1. Move that cup away from the table's edge. 
2. Let's make a list of tomorrow's tasks. 
3. My shoes' bottom is dirty. 
4. The colleagues of my husband are very competitive. 
5. Sally and Gina's hats are both very stylish. 
6. You can take notes on the other side of the paper. 
7. This should be resolved in a time of ten days. 
8. My friend's father's company is hiring. 
9. Have you seen Fred and Leo's new project? They worked on it together for 
months. 
10. My cat's favorite place to sleep is on the couch. 
(Answers at the end of this document) 
Summary 
• Some possessive pronouns have different forms depending on whether they 
are used before a noun, or after it / by themselves. Ex) That's my book / That 
book is mine 
• It's is short for "it is," and its signifies possession 
• If a noun is two words, add 's 
• If a noun is plural and ends in S, add only an apostrophe 
• If a singular noun ends in S, we sometimes add 's and sometimes only ' 
• For two people sharing possession, put the 's after the second name. Ex) Bill 
and Jen's house 
• For two people with separate possessions, put an 's after both names. Ex) 
Doug's and Steve's houses 
• With people, animals, time, and money, we typically use 's and not of. 
• With inanimate objects, we usually use of (although there are exceptions). 
• With people’s titles, we often use of (although there are sometimes 
alternatives). 


You’ve finished Lesson 21! Now try the exercises to get more practice with 
possessives. 
 
 
 
Writing Task 
Describe three of your favorite possessions. These could be things that are useful in 
your life, things that have sentimental value, or things that you worked hard to 
obtain. Why are they important to you? Send me your text at 
shayna@espressoenglish.net for feedback and correction!

lessons.title: Lesson 22
lessons.fullText:
Lesson 22 - Compound Nouns 
A compound noun is a noun that is composed of two or more words. 
Compound nouns can be: 
• One word – toothbrush, cupcake 
• Two words – flower pot, high school 
• A hyphenated word – self-esteem, merry-go-round 
There is no rule that defines which of these forms a compound noun takes, so if in 
doubt, check a dictionary. 
Compound nouns can be formed in a couple of different ways: 
Noun + Noun 
headphones 
paper clip 
apple tree 
Adjective + Noun 
blackboard 
greenhouse 
great-grandfather 
Verb-ing + Noun 
swimming pool 
washing machine 
frying pan 
Noun + Verb-ing 
bird watching 
ice skating 
Noun + Verb 
sunrise 
haircut 
rainfall 
Verb + Preposition 
getaway 
cutoff 
handout 
Preposition + Noun 
influx 
undergarments 
downtime 
 
Pronunciation of Compound Nouns 


When pronouncing compound nouns, the stress is usually on the first word: 
• HEADphones 
• PAPER clip 
• DOWNtime 
• GETaway 
• SWIMMING pool 
When saying the compound noun GREENhouse (a special transparent structure to 
grow plants) – the emphasis is on the word green. When saying GREEN HOUSE, 
there is approximately equal emphasis on both words, or a slightly stronger 
emphasis on “house.” 
There are occasional exceptions – in the word great-grandfather, the emphasis is on 
grandfather. But in general, compound nouns have the stress on the first word. 
Put it into practice! 
Can you guess the correct compound nouns for each of these things? 
belt buckle / belt clip / belt fasten 
 
footmark/ footprint / footstep 
 
billboard / signboard / showboard 


overpass / overstreet / overway 
 
frontlights / headlights / mainlights 
 
clearfish / jellyfish / waterfish 
 
kneecap / kneepoint / kneetip 


toothbit / toothpick / toothstick 
 
stopclock / stoptime / stopwatch 
 
skyscraper / skytoucher / skytopper 


black eye / blue eye / purple eye 
 
roller coaster / roller ride / roller flyer 
 
first aid / first help / first response 
 


Singular & Plural of Compound Nouns 
Notice that the first noun usually has the singular form. We say apple tree and not 
apples tree, even though the tree has many apples. We say toothbrush and not 
teethbrush, even though the brush is used on many teeth. 
There are a few exceptions: 
• a savings account 
(where you keep your money at the bank) 
• a customs officer 
(who checks to see if anyone is bringing illegal items into the country) 
• the arms trade 
(“arms” = weapons, “trade” = buying and selling) 
• a glasses case 
(a protective case for your glasses) 
• a clothesline 
(where you can hang your clothes to dry) 
• an arts festival 
(involves multiple arts) 
• a publications department 
(part of a company that produces publications) 
• a news broadcast 
(the word “news” always has an “s”) 
Another exception is when the first noun is a user of the second noun – in this case, 
we often use 's: 
• a bird's nest, a lion's den, a girls' school, the men's room 
When talking about parts of the body, we use 's for the possessive form:  
• the lady's hair 
• the boy's arms 
But when talking about parts of objects, we usually use a noun + noun compound 
word, or "of": 
• a table leg 
a table’s leg 
• the TV screen 


• a shirt collar 
• a branch of the company 
• the lid of the jar 
Notice this difference when talking about cups and glasses: 
• a tea cup refers to the empty cup itself 
• a cup of tea is full of tea 
• a wine glass refers to the empty glass itself 
• a glass of wine is full of wine 
Now, what if we want to make a compound noun plural? 
We usually just add –s to the final word: 
• toothbrushes 
• paper clips 
• apple trees 
• swimming pools 
• vice-presidents 
If it’s a structure using “of,” add –s to the main word: 
• two cups of tea 
• two cup of teas 
• three Ministers of Defense 
• three Minister of Defenses 
As always, we have some exceptions! 
Singular 
Plural 
Meaning 
passer-by 
passers-by 
A person walking past a place 
brother-in-law 
sister-in-law 
brothers-in-law 
sisters-in-law 
The brothers or sisters of your 
husband/wife 
bird of prey 
birds of prey 
A bird that eats other animals 
commander-
in-chief 
commanders-in-
chief 
A person with authority in the military 
runner-up 
runners-up 
A person who did not win a competition, but 
finished in second place (or 3rd, 4th, 5th) 
 


Nouns Formed from Phrasal Verbs 
Some nouns are formed from phrasal verbs. The phrasal verb is two words, and the 
noun is one word, for example: 
• Can you hand out these papers? 
• I need to print some handouts for class. 
• I mixed up the documents. 
• Sorry about the mix-up. 
• The airline is giving away a free round-trip ticket. 
• Let’s enter the giveaway to see if we’ll win! 
This can’t be done for every phrasal verb. For example, another word for “hand out” 
is “give out,” yet there is no such noun as “giveout.”  
Here are 10 examples of compound nouns formed from phrasal verbs. See if you can 
guess their meaning from the context: 
1) Tryouts for the local baseball team will be held one month before the season 
starts. 
2) The movie was great, but the ending was a bit of a letdown. 
3) Public health officials are working to combat a sudden outbreak of disease. 
4) The CEO’s poor decisions led to the downfall of the company. 
5) I really like the layout of this website; it’s easy to find things. 
6) This seaside hotel is the perfect place to spend a weekend getaway. 
7) After Christmas dinner, we had a lot of leftovers in the fridge. 
8) There have been problems with this project ever since the outset. 
9) I had a religious upbringing. 
10) 
Both sides blamed each other for the breakdown of negotiations. 
 
You’ve finished Lesson 22! Now try the exercises for more practice with compound 
nouns. 
 
 
Image sources: Nevit Dilman, Myke2020, Coolcaesar, ANT Berezhnyi, Dan90266, 
Shannon Moore, Baycrest, WikiFB3  


Quiz – Lesson 22 – Compound Nouns 
Here are a number of compound nouns. Some of them you might already know, 
others might be new to you. Try to put each one in the correct sentence!

1. Everyone stayed in the ___________________________ and danced until 4 AM. 
2. If your back hurts, you can take a ___________________________ to feel better. 
3. The Titanic sank after it hit a giant ___________________________ in the middle of 
the ocean. 
4. I don't remember the recipe exactly - I'll have to check the 
___________________________. 
5. A government ___________________________ explained the policy change. 
6. The ___________________________  gave me a discount because I bought three 
things. 
7. Make sure to bring ___________________________, otherwise you'll end up with a ton 
of mosquito bites. 
8. I don't particularly like seafood, especially ___________________________. 
9. This environmentally-protected area is a home to various types of 
___________________________. 
10. I left my ___________________________ and moved to the big city when I was 18. 
11. That boy is always disobeying his parents. He's a real ___________________________. 
12. In the movie, an alien ___________________________ attacks and destroys the capital 
city. 


13. Although it was nighttime, we were able to see clearly because of the bright 
___________________________. 
14. We came to a ___________________________ and weren't sure whether to turn right 
or left. 
15. The building's heating system is broken - we'll need to call a 
___________________________. 
16. One ___________________________ of winning the lottery is that all your friends and 
relatives start asking you for money. 
17. My favorite team was losing 2-0, but they made a ___________________________ and 
ended up winning 3-2. 
18. The ___________________________ of the evening was getting an autograph from my 
favorite actress! 
19. One of my favorite things to eat in the summer is a nice, juicy piece of 
___________________________. 
20. I passed the ball to my ___________________________ and he scored the winning 
goal. 
 
 
Writing Task 
As society changes, the language changes as well. Today many of the compound 
nouns for people’s professions, which used to end with “man,” are being modified – 
for example, we have fireman, firewoman, and the gender-neutral firefighter.  
In your country, which jobs are considered more as “men’s jobs” and which jobs are 
considered “women’s jobs”? Is this changing at all? What difficulties do you imagine 
someone faces when they have a profession that is considered “typical” of the 
opposite gender? Send me your text at shayna@espressoenglish.net for feedback 
and correction! 


Answers – Quiz – Lesson 22  
1. Everyone stayed in the nightclub and danced until 4 AM. 
2. If your back hurts, you can take a painkiller to feel better. 
3. The Titanic sank after it hit a giant iceberg in the middle of the ocean. 
4. I don't remember the recipe exactly - I'll have to check the cookbook. 
5. A government spokesperson explained the policy change. 
6. The saleswoman gave me a discount because I bought three things. 
7. Make sure to bring bug spray, otherwise you'll end up with a ton of mosquito 
bites. 
8. I don't particularly like seafood, especially shellfish. 
9. This environmentally-protected area is a home to various types of wildlife. 
10. I left my hometown and moved to the big city when I was 18. 
11. That boy is always disobeying his parents. He's a real troublemaker. 
12. In the movie, an alien spaceship attacks and destroys the capital city. 
13. Although it was nighttime, we were able to see clearly because of the bright 
moonlight. 
14. We came to a crossroads and weren't sure whether to turn right or left. 
15. The building's heating system is broken - we'll need to call a repairman. 
16. One downside of winning the lottery is that all your friends and relatives 
start asking you for money. 
17. My favorite team was losing 2-0, but they made a comeback and ended up 
winning 3-2. 
18. The highlight of the evening was getting an autograph from my favorite 
actress! 
19. One of my favorite things to eat in the summer is a nice, juicy piece of 
watermelon. 
20. I passed the ball to my teammate and he scored the winning goal.

lessons.title: Lesson 23
lessons.fullText:
Lesson 23: There & It 
Use there when we talk about something for the first time, to say that it exists: 
• There's a new café on Main Street. 
• There are several books in my backpack. 
• There were eight applicants for the job. 
• There has been a change in plans. 
• There will be a lot of people at the concert. 
As you can see, you can use there with different forms of the verb to be to talk 
about things in the past, present, and future. 
Use it to refer to something we have mentioned previously. 
• We went to the new café. It’s really nice. 
• How was the traffic?  
It was terrible. 
• I read the book and I really liked it. 
Compare these examples to see the difference between there and it: 
• There’s a package waiting for you at home. 
• There’s a package waiting for you at home. It was delivered this morning. 
• There was a typo in the document. 
• I found a typo in the document and fixed it. 
Simple, right? Let’s look at each one in more detail. 
There 
Negative forms 
To talk about the absence of something, you can say it one of two ways: 
• There’s no milk in the fridge. 
• There isn’t any milk in the fridge. 
• There was nobody in the office. 
• There wasn’t anybody in the office. 
• There are no batteries in the toy. 
• There aren’t any batteries in the toy. 


However, be sure to avoid mixing them and creating a double negative! 
• There isn’t no milk in the fridge. 
• There wasn’t nobody in the office. 
 
Singular and plural 
We can abbreviate there is to there’s. However, we cannot abbreviate there are to 
there’re (even though it often sounds like this in spoken English): 
• There’s a bird in the tree. 
• There are two birds in the tree. 
Sounds like: Therere two birds in the tree. 
When you have a series of two, three, or more single objects, we use there is (not 
there are): 
• There is an apple and a banana in the bowl. 
• There's a pencil, an eraser, and some paper on the desk. 
If one of the objects in the list is plural, then we say there is or there are based oon 
the noun closest to it: 
• There’s a dog and two cats in the yard. 
• There are two cats and a dog in the yard. 
To use there with a lot of or lots of, it depends on whether the following noun is 
uncountable or plural/countable: 
• There’s a lot of frosting on the cake. 
• There are a lot of cookies in the box. 
• There’s lots of information in this book. 
• There are lots of articles about this topic. 
In informal English, some people simply use there’s all the time, even with plural 
nouns. This is not correct, but it is common: 
• There’s a lot of fun things to do in this town. 
• There’s about twenty children in the class. 
 


Put it into practice! 
There’s or there are? 
1. ____________________ a few things I need to do before I leave. 
2. ____________________ a little bit of snow on the ground. 
3. ____________________ nothing inside the box. 
4. ____________________ some interesting after-school activities available. 
5. ____________________ lots of violence in that neighborhood. 
6. ____________________ a mirror and several pictures on the wall. 
7. ____________________ two cookies and some ice cream in the bowl. 
There with other verbs 
You can also use there with modal verbs in the present: 
• There must be something we can do to help. 
• Don’t put your hand into that hole. There might/could be a snake in there. 
• There should be some books about Roman history in the library. 
And with modal verbs in the past: 
• There must have been tons of fans waiting for the celebrity when he arrived. 
• The road is closed. There might have been an accident. 
• There should have been a team of five people helping the customers; how 
come only two of you were working? 
As well as with a few state verbs: 
• There appears/seems to be a problem with the internet. 
• There tend to be more tourists in the area in January. 
 
It 
As mentioned earlier in the lesson, we use it for something we have already 
mentioned – but let me caution you about two common mistakes. One is forgetting 
to use it when the sentence needs a subject, or when the verb needs an object: 
• I bought a new jacket. Is black. 
• My microwave broke, but my husband fixed. 


The other common mistake is repeating "it" immediately after the subject was first 
mentioned – this is unnecessary: 
• The food it’s is not very good. 
• My favorite book it’s is War and Peace. 
So here are four situations where we use it in English: 
1. As the subject of a sentence when we have mentioned the 
thing recently. 
This can be in two separate sentences, or in the same sentence when beginning a 
new clause: 
• Where’s my wallet? It’s not in my purse. 
• I bought a shirt for my son, but it was too small. 
2. As the direct object with verbs that need a direct object, and 
we have mentioned the thing recently. 
Again, this can be in two separate sentences or in the same one: 
• Is the window still open? 
No, I closed it. 
• I caught the ball, but then I dropped it. 
3. In expressions with distance, time, and weather: 
• How far is it to Boston? 
It's about five miles. 
• How long does it take to change a tire? 
It takes 10 minutes. 
• It's a nice day. 
• It's raining. 
• It was sunny. 
• It will be cloudy. 
4. Use it as the subject when the subject is a long clause 
• It's not fair that she's getting paid more than me for the same work. 


• It was surprising that he was able to accomplish his goal. 
= The fact that he was able to accomplish his goal was surprising. 
• It hasn’t been proven whether or not he committed the crime. 
This structure is often used with emotions: 
• It annoys me when people use up the toilet paper and don’t replace the roll. 
• It’s shocking that such blatant lies are taught in school. 
• It was inspiring to see how many people donated to the animal shelter. 
We also have the structures I like/love/enjoy/hate (it) when… - in these 
sentences, it is optional, but most native speakers include it: 
 
• I love it when my kids offer to wash the dishes. 
= I love when my kids offer to wash the dishes. 
• I hate it when people don’t return my calls. 
• I can’t stand it when you take my stuff without asking! 
We also tend to use it with some verbs of judgment: 
• It’s good that you’re studying English every day. 
• It’s a shame that you missed the party. 
• It’s wonderful when someone believes in your potential. 
• It’s terrible when people turn a blind eye to child abuse. 
And some verbs of perception and interpretation: 
• It seems like you’re upset. Is everything OK? 
• Ouch. It feels like I pulled a muscle in my back. 
• I find it difficult to understand Australian English. 
= I find understanding Australian English difficult. 
• It hit me / It dawned on me that he’d been right all along. 
These expressions mean “I realized” or “I suddenly understood” 
• I think/believe/consider it an advantage that our company is small.  
• I see/regard it as a lack of respect when people are late for appointments. 
 
 
 


Put it into practice! 
Are these eight sentences correct or incorrect? 
1. If you want to go to the city center, is a half-hour drive. 
2. Is it expensive to get solar panels installed? 
3. My brother's birthday it's in April. 
4. It's amazing that she speaks six languages fluently. 
5. Look at that rainbow! It's beautiful! 
6. Is not good when people are excluded because of their race. 
7. The latest episode was great! Have you seen? 
8. My cat likes it when I rub her belly. 
(Answers at the end of this document) 
Summary 
• Use there to talk about something for the first time. Use it to refer back to 
something we have already mentioned. 
• There can be used with various forms of the word to be, as well as modal 
verbs and some state verbs like seems or appears. 
• Say there's with singular nouns and uncountable nouns. Say there are with 
plural nouns. 
• When you have items in a list, the word there matches the first noun closest 
to it. 
• Use it in four situations: 
o As the subject of a sentence or clause, when we have mentioned the 
thing recently. Ex) I bought a new jacket. It’s black. 
o As the direct object with verbs that need one, when we have mentioned 
the thing recently. Ex) I caught the ball, but then I dropped it. 
o In expressions with distance, time, and weather 
o When the subject is a long clause 
 
You’ve finished Lesson 23! Now try the practice exercises to review what you’ve 
learned in today’s lesson. 
 


Quiz – Lesson 23 – There & It 
Circle the correct word to complete each sentence! 
1. That milk has been in the fridge for two weeks, so it / there might have gone 
bad. 
2. It's / There's a closet, a lamp, and two single beds in the hotel room. 
3. It / There bothers me when I can't find something I had just a moment ago. 
4. You can borrow my phone charger. It / there should be compatible with your 
phone. 
5. It / There seems to be a leak somewhere in the plumbing. 
6. It/ There was a bad idea to travel without making plans in advance. 
7. It's / There's a pebble in my shoe and it's / there's hurting my foot. 
8. The President is staying in that hotel, so it's / there's lots of extra security. 
9. If you need to get gas, it's / there's a station just around the corner. 
10. Right now it's / there's spring, and there's / there are flowers everywhere. 
11. Is it / there cold outside? 
12. That case is very mysterious, but it / there must be a logical explanation. 
13. Is it / there any ice cream in the freezer? 
14. Yesterday it / there was an earthquake in California. 
15. It's / There's great when you can resolve a conflict peacefully. 
16. It's / There's been a long time since I last saw my grandparents. 
 
Writing Task 
Describe some of the interesting places in your city or country… or, if you prefer, the 
city or country where you currently live. Use “there is,” “there are,” and “it” when 
appropriate to talk about the things a tourist should see. Send your text at 
shayna@espressoenglish.net for feedback and correction!

lessons.title: Lesson 24
lessons.fullText:
Lesson 24:  
Reflexive and Emphatic Pronouns 
In today’s lesson, you’ll learn how to use words like myself, herself, themselves, 
etc. These words can be used as reflexive pronouns or emphatic pronouns.  
Reflexive Pronouns 
We use reflexive pronouns when the subject and object of the action are the 
same: 
• He saw me. 
He = subject / me = object 
• I saw me myself in the mirror. 
I am both the subject and the object 
• Mary told George not to worry. 
Mary = subject / George = object 
• Mary told her herself not to worry. 
Mary is both the subject and the object. 
• They bought their kids some toys. 
They = subject / their kids = object 
• They bought themselves some new clothes. 
They purchased the clothes for their own use 
Subject 
Reflexive 
Example 
I 
myself 
I saw myself in the mirror 
you 
yourself (singular) 
yourselves (plural) 
Be careful so that you don’t hurt yourself. 
Okay, kids, I expect you to behave yourselves. 
he 
himself 
He introduced himself to the audience. 
she 
herself 
She stopped herself before she made a mistake. 
it 
itself 
History tends to repeat itself. 
one 
oneself 
One should be able to laugh at oneself. 
we 
ourselves 
We enjoyed ourselves at the party. 
they 
themselves 
They prepared themselves for the trip. 
 


Put it into practice! 
Which reflexive pronoun should go in the blank? 
1. The children amused ________________ by playing with the dog. 
2. Karina is teaching ________________ how to paint. 
3. He went into the kitchen and poured _______________ a drink. 
4. If you have a complaint, keep it to __________________. 
5. I gave ________________ a haircut – it didn’t turn out very well. 
6. We blame ________________ for the mistake. 
7. This coffee machine can clean ________________ automatically. 
(Answers at the end of this document) 
Differently from some other languages, we don't usually use -self with the verbs 
wash, shave, or dress: 
• I washed my face / my hands. / I took a shower. 
I washed myself. 
• He shaves himself every morning. 
• She got dressed. 
She dressed herself. 
Sometimes we do say “dress oneself” when talking about a child who is learning this 
basic skill, or someone who has difficulty: 
• After his injury, he wasn’t able to dress himself without help. 
• My daughter managed to dress herself this morning. 
Here are some verbs that are often used with reflexive pronouns: 
• amuse yourself  
= provide your own entertainment 
• enjoy yourself  
= have a good time 
• content yourself with  
= be satisfied with something, even if it is not exactly what you wanted or 
expected. Ex) I wanted to sell my bike for $200, but I had to content myself with 
$150. 
• behave yourself  
= behave well 


• cut/hurt/kill yourself 
• introduce yourself 
= present yourself to another person 
• teach yourself  
= when you are your own teacher 
• tell yourself / talk to yourself / think to yourself 
If you tell yourself something, it can be speaking aloud or simply thinking it 
If you talk to yourself, it means you are speaking aloud  
If you think to yourself, it means you have thoughts without sharing them with 
anyone 
• help yourself 
If you tell someone “help yourself” to some food for example, you are telling 
them to take as much as they want.  
• get yourself / buy yourself  
To “get yourself” something is to get something for yourself, and to “buy 
yourself” something is to buy something for your own use. 
• find yourself = suddenly realize you are in a certain situation. Ex) I spent more 
and more and one day I found myself with nothing in my bank account. 
• see yourself = your own opinion of yourself.  
Ex) He always sees himself as the victim. 
 
Here are some examples of “self” words being used with other prepositions: 
• You shouldn't just follow others' opinions, you should think for yourself. 
• We took one magazine for our son and another for ourselves. 
• I wrapped the blanket around myself. 
• The politicians were talking amongst themselves. 
• He’s so arrogant; he’s always talking about himself. 
• She doesn’t care about anybody but herself. 
Do not use the “self” words when somebody brings/takes something with them: 
• It’s pretty dark. I’ll take a flashlight with myself me. 
• Margaret is coming over tonight; I’m not sure if she’s bringing her kids with 
herself her. 
 


Put it into practice! 
• What was the last thing you bought for yourself? 
I bought myself ______________________ 
• What do you tell yourself when you're facing a stressful situation? 
I tell myself ________________________ 
• What was the last situation in which you enjoyed yourself? 
I enjoyed myself at ___________________________ 
• Have you ever taught yourself something? 
I’ve taught myself ____________________________ 
 
Emphatic Pronouns 
These “self” words can also be used to emphasize the importance of that specific 
person doing the action, for example: 
• The President himself gave me the award. 
(it was the President, and not another person) 
• My daughter baked these cookies herself! 
• Give me the letter - I'll deliver it myself. 
• The teachers themselves are great, but the school administrators are 
terrible. (specifying the teachers and distinguishing them from the 
administrators) 
When we use a “self” pronoun for emphasis, we often place it either at the end of the 
phrase (more common), or immediately after the subject: 
• The President gave me the award himself. 
• The President himself gave me the award. 
If we include the word “by” before the “self” word, that changes the meaning – it 
means alone or without any help: 
• I walked home by myself. 
• He's shy. He's just standing there in the corner all by himself. 
• You’re not strong enough to move the refrigerator by yourself. 
 


Put it into practice! 
• What's one thing you always do yourself; you don’t want anyone else to do it 
for you? 
I always ________________________ myself. 
• When was the last time you spent time by yourself? 
I _________________________________ by myself. 
 
Summary 
• We use reflexive pronouns when the subject and object of the action are the 
same person. Ex) I saw myself in the mirror. 
• We don't usually use -self words with wash, shave, or dress, or with 
bring/take something with (someone). 
• These “self” words can also be used to emphasize the importance of that 
specific person doing the action. Ex) The President himself gave me the 
award. 
• If we include the word “by” before the “self” word, that changes the meaning – 
it means alone or without any help. Ex) I walked home by myself. 
 
You’ve finished Lesson 24! Now try the exercises for more practice with these “self” 
pronouns.

(myself, himself, ourselves, etc.)

3. Mr. Jones _______________  __________________  from the meeting in order to take a 
phone call. 
4. Pamela is very confident. She _______________  __________________. 
5. I didn't mean to eat so much, but I just couldn't _______________  __________________. 
6. I took a deep breath and _______________  __________________ to stay calm. 
7. She always gets nervous during interviews and feels like she can't 
_______________  __________________  very well. 
8. My grandmother is very old, but she can still _______________  __________________ 
9. I'm learning first aid so that I can be prepared just in case my kids 
_______________  __________________. 
10. He _______________  __________________  a salad for lunch. 
11. You should learn self-defense so that you can _______________  __________________. 
12. A bird _______________  __________________ trapped in our attic, and couldn't find its

13. My son _______________  __________________ after getting good grades in his first 
semester of college. 
14. We _______________  our house _______________ . 
15. After his girlfriend dumped him, Mike spent several weeks _______________  
__________________. 


Writing Task 
Some people and cultures strongly value independence and self-sufficiency, and 
others put a higher priority on relationships and depending on each other.  
Which way do you tend to be? Do you prefer doing things by yourself, or working on 
a team… and why? Give an example of a project or other task you have done in the 
past (either by yourself or with the help of others) and talk about how it turned out. 
Send me your text at shayna@espressoenglish.net for feedback and correction! 
 
Answers – Quiz – Lesson 24 
1. My husband and I bought ourselves some camping gear. 
2. You can feel free to help yourself to anything from the refrigerator. 
3. Mr. Jones excused himself from the meeting in order to take a phone call. 
4. Pamela is very confident. She believes in herself.

15. 
After his girlfriend dumped him, Mike spent several weeks feeling 
sorry for himself.

lessons.title: Lesson 25
lessons.fullText:
Lesson 25: Position of Adjectives 
Adjectives are words that describe nouns. We can use adjectives before the noun, or 
following a linking verb such as appear, be, become, get, feel, look, seem: 
• Her eyes are blue. 
• She has blue eyes. 
• This bread looks fresh. 
• Fresh bread is delicious. 
Some adjectives are never used before the noun; they are only used after the linking 
verb: 
• The boy was alone in the room. 
The alone boy 
• The baby is asleep. 
The asleep baby 
• The leaders seem to be aware of the problem. 
The aware leaders 
These include a number of "a" words like afraid, alike, alive, alone, ashamed, 
asleep, awake, and aware. Usually these adjectives have another version that we 
can put before the noun: 
• The child was afraid. 
The frightened child ran to his mother. 
• The boy was alone. 
A lone boy sat in the classroom. 
• These two books seem very much alike. 
I've read two similar books lately. 
• The baby is asleep. 
The sleeping baby is wrapped in a blanket. 
One exception to the “adjectives before nouns” rule is that adjectives come after 
words like something, anybody, nothing: 
• I want to go someplace warm on vacation. 
• There's nothing interesting in the news. 
 


And a few nouns ending in -able/-ible can also be used after nouns: 
• We're prepared for every situation imaginable. 
We're prepared for every imaginable situation. 
• He took the last seat available. 
He took the last available seat. 
 
Order of Adjectives 
Which is correct? 
• They bought a nice new car 
• They bought a new nice car 
If that was too easy, try these: 
• It's an ____________ ____________ _____________ ____________ ____________ mug. 
ceramic / brown / coffee / old / ugly 
• She was wearing a ____________ ____________ ____________ ____________ skirt. 
black / cute / leather / little 
What do you notice about the first adjective in each series? Is it an opinion 
adjective or a fact adjective? 
It’s an opinion adjective. The first rule to remember is that opinion adjectives 
usually come before fact adjectives. 
Some other examples of opinion adjectives include: 
• good / bad / great / terrible 
• beautiful / pretty / sexy / comfortable 
• ugly / awful / strange / uncomfortable 
• delicious / disgusting / tasty / nasty 
• important / excellent / wonderful / brilliant 
• funny / interesting / boring 
Put it into practice! 
Each of these phrases has two adjectives for you to put in the correct order. 
Remember – opinions before facts: 


1. __________________ _________________ food 
delicious / Mexican 
2. a __________________ _________________ flower 
yellow / beautiful 
3. a(n) __________________ _________________ theory 
important / new 
4. a __________________ _________________ coin 
silver / valuable 
5. a(n) __________________ _________________ painting 
abstract / brilliant 
6. a(n) __________________ _________________ man 
interesting / young 
OK, so now you know that opinion adjectives usually go first. But what about the fact 
adjectives? In general, the correct order of adjectives in English is this: 
1 
2 
3 
4 
5 
6 
7 
8 
Opinion 
Size 
big, small, 
large, little, 
short, huge, 
tiny, gigantic 
Shape 
round, 
square, 
flat, 
triangular
Age 
old, new, 
young, 
ancient 
Color 
red, 
blue, 
green, 
yellow 
Nationality/Origin 
Italian, Japanese, 
Thai, German, 
French 
Material 
silver, 
cotton, 
wooden, 
metal, 
plastic 
Purpose 
 
 
“Purpose” adjectives are almost like part of the noun itself. They describe its 
function or what it is used for: 
• running shoes 
• a sleeping bag 
• a flower vase 
• a frying pan 
• a tennis racket 
It’s rare to use more than 3 adjectives. But the adjectives you do use should follow 
this order approximately. There may be some exceptions! 


With time adjectives, we put first/next/last or past before the number: 
• the first two weeks 
the two first weeks 
• the past ten minutes 
the ten past minutes 
 
Whether or not to use and 
When there are two or more color adjectives, use and: 
• yellow and orange flowers 
• a red, white, and blue flag 
We usually don't use and with other adjectives if they are before a noun: 
• a round wooden table 
a round and wooden table 
• long brown hair 
long and brown hair 
However, we can use and with other adjectives if they are after the noun: 
• The day was hot and humid. 
• The clouds were big, white, and fluffy. 
There are other adjectives that don’t fall into the categories above. For these, the 
essential rule to remember is that opinion adjectives always come before fact 
adjectives (appearance and other descriptive adjectives): 
• delicious (opinion) organic (fact) food 
• crazy (opinion) religious (fact) people 
• interesting (opinion) cultural (fact) traditions 
• confusing (opinion) financial (fact) data 
Although studying the order of adjectives in English can help… there reaches a point 
where you’ll learn them best simply by seeing and hearing them in action.  
Most native English speakers don’t know the rules of adjective order at all – we just 
know that it “sounds right” to say “the big red ball” and “sounds wrong” to say “the 
red big ball.” 


Compound Adjectives 
Some adjectives have more than one word. For example: 
• a well-known author 
• an English-speaking country 
• a three-hour movie 
• a part-time job 
• a middle-aged woman 
These are called compound adjectives. When they are before a noun, we use a 
hyphen – but when they are after a noun and the verb “to be” or another linking 
verb, we do not: 
• This is a world-famous museum. 
This museum is world famous. 
• It was quite a thought-provoking book. 
The book was quite thought provoking. 
The exception is with adverbs ending in –LY. These do not require a hyphen: 
• He is a widely recognized expert. 
• His work is widely recognized.  
There is an additional detail with compound adjectives involving numbers – when 
they are before the noun, we do not include –s: 
• I have a ten-year-old daughter. 
My daughter is ten years old. 
• Let’s take a five-minute break. 
Let’s take a break for five minutes. 
In addition to numbers, compound adjectives often include the past participle or 
present participle: 
With past participle 
With present participle 
well-known author 
ready-made meals 
old-fashioned furniture 
a tree-lined path 
a fast-growing economy 
far-reaching effects 
a never-ending process 
a time-saving tool 
 


There are many other compounds that include other words as well: 
• ice-cold lemonade 
• long-term plan 
• a Boston-based company 
• last-minute changes 
For more compound adjectives and example sentences, visit the link in the lesson 
text: http:///compound-adjectives-in-english/ 
 
Put it into practice! 
Can you connect these words to form compound adjectives? 
 
Summary 
• Adjectives describe nouns. They can be placed immediately before the noun 
(blue eyes) or after the verb "to be" or another linking verb (Her eyes are 
blue). 
• Some adjectives, such as afraid and alone, cannot be placed immediately 
before the noun - they must be after a linking verb. 
• A few words ending in -able and -ible can be placed either before or after the 
noun, for example: the last seat available / the last available seat 
• When there are multiple adjectives, opinion adjectives come before fact 
adjectives. 


• The fact adjectives usually follow the order of Size, Shape, Age, Color, 
Nationality/Origin, Material, Purpose 
• When adjectives come before the noun, we only use the word and between 
two color adjectives: 
o a red and yellow jacket 
o the old, run-down house 
• When they come after the noun, then we can use and: 
o the house was old and run-down 
• Compound adjectives are made of two words, and they often contain the 
past or present participle: well-known, long-lasting 
• If they are before the noun, we use a hyphen; if they are after the noun and 
a linking verb, we do not. 
You’ve finished Lesson 25! Now try the exercises to get more practice with 
adjectives. 
 
 
Writing Task 
Describe a detailed scene – it could be… 
• a favorite place 
• an cultural tradition or holiday 
• an interesting experience 
• etc. 
Try to include lots of details and use many descriptive adjectives, keeping the rules 
for their position and order in mind. Send me your text at 
shayna@espressoenglish.net for feedback and correction!

Answers – Quiz – Lesson 25 
1. Put the bottles in the large green recycling bin. 
2. There's a nasty black oil stain on the floor of the garage.

lessons.title: Lesson 26
lessons.fullText:
Lesson 26:  
Gradable & Non-Gradable Adjectives 
Some adjectives in English are gradable - that means you can have different degrees 
or levels of that quality. For example, the weather can be:  
• a little cold 
• rather cold 
• very cold 
• extremely cold. 
Other adjectives are non-gradable – meaning we can’t have different degrees or 
levels of that quality. There are three types of non-gradable adjectives. 
Extreme Adjectives 
Extreme adjectives are words that mean “extremely + adjective” – for example, 
freezing means “extremely cold.” The weather can’t be “a little bit freezing” or “very 
freezing” – because the word “freezing” itself automatically means “extremely cold.” 
“Huge” means “extremely big.” Again, it’s not possible for something to be “slightly 
huge” or “very huge” – the definition of the word “huge” itself is “extremely big.” 
Put it into practice! 
Which one is the extreme adjective? 
1. bad / terrible 
2. clean / spotless 
3. fascinating / interesting 
4. hilarious / funny 
5. hungry / starving 
6. ancient / old 
7. exhausted / tired 
8. astonishing / surprising 
(Answers at the end of this document) 
 


Absolute Adjectives 
Another type of non-gradable adjective is called an absolute adjective.  
These are words that are either “yes or no.” For example, the word dead – you can’t 
be “a little bit dead” or “very dead” – either YES, you are dead, or NO, you’re not 
dead. Here are a few other examples: 
• unique / not unique 
• perfect / imperfect 
• impossible / possible 
• pregnant / not pregnant 
Put it into practice!  
Which one is the absolute adjective? 
1. mysterious / unknown 
2. essential / important 
3. common / universal 
4. equal / similar 
5. ideal / useful 
(Answers at the end of this document) 
Classifying Adjectives 
A third type of non-gradable adjective is a classifying adjective, which describes 
what type or category something is: 
• an electric stove or gas stove 
• a daily meeting or a weekly meeting 
• a wooden chair or a plastic chair 
Again, we can’t have a “slightly electric stove” or a “very plastic chair.” 
Put it into practice! 
Which one is the classifying adjective? 
1. a dangerous weapon / an atomic weapon 
2. a pine tree / a tall tree 


3. a government worker / a well-paid worker 
4. a comfortable shirt / a silk shirt 
5. an American tradition / an interesting tradition 
(Answers at the end of this document) 
 
Differences in using Gradable  
and Non-Gradable Adjectives 
1) No comparatives / superlatives with non-gradable adjectives 
With regular adjectives, we can use comparatives and superlatives to compare two 
or more things: 
• My house is big. 
• My neighbor’s house is bigger than mine.  
(comparative) 
• My parents’ house is the biggest house on the street. 
(superlative) 
• His idea is important. 
• Her idea is more important. 
• My idea is the most important of all. 
With extreme adjectives, we usually don’t use comparatives and superlatives: 
• My parents’ house is enormous. 
• My parents’ house is more enormous / the most enormous. 
It's the same for absolute and classifying adjectives. It's impossible for one dead 
person to be "deader" than another, or for one plastic chair to be "more plastic" than 
another. 
2) Use different adverbs with non-gradable adjectives. 
With gradable adjectives, we can use adverbs of degree like these: 
• Small degree: a little, a bit, slightly 
• Middle degree: fairly, rather, somewhat 
• Large degree: very, extremely, immensely, intensely, hugely, quite 


For example: 
• I’m rather hungry. 
I’m very hungry. 
• Your shoes are slightly dirty. 
This room is extremely dirty. 
• We’re a little tired. 
We’re immensely tired. 
With non-gradable adjectives, we CANNOT use these adverbs: 
• I’m very starving. 
• Your work is slightly perfect. 
• My watch is somewhat digital. 
However, we can use the adverbs absolutely, completely, and utterly to give 
additional emphasis to the non-gradable adjective: 
• I’m absolutely furious. 
• We’re completely exhausted. 
• The movie was utterly terrifying. 
These are often used with extreme adjectives. With absolute and classifying 
adjectives, they can be used with some, but not others: 
• That’s absolutely impossible. 
They’re absolutely married. 
• This car is completely electric. 
The conference is completely annual. 
We also tend not to use absolutely, completely, or utterly with regular gradable 
adjectives: 
• It’s absolutely cold today. 
It’s extremely cold today. 
• She’s completely friendly. 
She’s really friendly. 
• This is utterly easy. 
This is very easy. 


The more informal words pretty and really, can be used with gradable adjectives 
and with SOME non-gradable adjectives – again, usually the extreme ones, but not 
the absolute or classifying ones: 
• This room is pretty dirty. (gradable) 
• This room is pretty filthy. (extreme) 
• The party is really crowded. (gradable) 
• The party is really packed. (extreme) 
• Those facts are really unknown. 
• Those are pretty military vehicles. 
Other words that can be used with some non-gradable adjectives include totally, 
nearly/almost, virtually, and quite: 
• He was nearly dead. 
• That's totally impossible. 
• This technology is virtually unique. 
• This philosophy is quite universal. 
You can see that these are absolute and extreme adjectives, not classifying 
adjectives. With classifying adjectives, we can sometimes use the words entirely, 
completely, fully, largely, and mainly to say that all or most of the things fall into 
that category: 
• This food is completely organic. 
• This system is fully digital. 
• The staff is entirely American. 
• The staff is largely Chinese. 
• The material is mainly cotton. 
Now, with that said...  these rules are not 100% and occasionally you will encounter 
native speakers using combinations that don't seem to follow them, like "most 
unique," “very pregnant,” "rather exhausted," or "somewhat true." 
Both Gradable and Non-Gradable 
A few adjectives have both gradable and non-gradable meanings: 
• This is a very common problem. 
common = frequently found (gradable) 


• We have a lot of common interests. 
common = shared 
• That vase is very old. 
old = created a long time ago (gradable) 
• I saw my old teacher yesterday. 
old = former 
Other adjectives sometimes function as a descriptive (gradable) adjective, and other 
times function as an absolute or classifying adjective: 
• It was a rather wild party. 
(descriptive & gradable) 
• A lion is a wild animal. 
(classifying) 
• He takes a very scientific approach in his article. 
(descriptive & gradable) 
• We need more funding for scientific research. 
(classifying) 
• She had a slightly guilty expression on her face. 
(descriptive & gradable) 
• The criminal was found to be guilty. 
(absolute) 
Put it into practice!  
In which sentence can you insert the adverb? 
slightly 
• His accent sounded __________ foreign. 
• We need to reform __________ foreign policy. 
rather 
• Go away. This is ___________ private property. 
• He's a __________ private person. 
very 
• Is that a(n) _____________ original painting or a reproduction? 
• That's a ____________ original idea! 


Summary 
We have four types of adjectives: 
• Gradable adjectives (warm, tall, comfortable) 
• Extreme adjectives (freezing, tiny, ancient) 
• Absolute adjectives (dead, pregnant, impossible) 
• Classifying adjectives (wooden, digital, annual) 
We can use adverbs of degree (slightly, rather, very) with gradable adjectives. 
With extreme adjectives, we can add emphasis with absolutely, completely, and 
utterly. 
We can use really, fairly, and pretty with both gradable and extreme adjectives. 
Other words that can be used with some non-gradable adjectives include totally, 
nearly/almost, virtually, and quite. 
With classifying adjectives, we can sometimes use the words entirely, completely, 
fully, largely, and mainly. 
Some adjectives are gradable in some situations, and non-gradable in others. 
You’ve finished Lesson 26! 
Now try the exercises, because practicing these combinations of adjectives is the 
best way to remember them. 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Quiz – Lesson 26 
Complete five of the sentences with the word very, and the other five with one of the 
following words: entirely / almost / absolutely / practically / completely. 
Sometimes more than one answer is possible. 
1. Your explanation was ___________________________ clear; I understood everything 
perfectly. 
2. My neighbor drives a Ferrari. He's ___________________________ rich. 
3. I was ___________________________ thrilled when I received the award. 
4. The renovation of the school is ___________________________ complete - there are 
only about two more weeks of work left. 
5. He responded to the situation in a(n) ___________________________ immature way. 
6. The whole experience was ___________________________ humiliating. 
7. The medicine has some ___________________________ strong side effects. 
8. Until last year, the company's board of directors was ___________________________ 
male. 
9. The unemployment rate is ___________________________ high due to the global 
economic crisis. 
10. This hearing aid is so small that it's ___________________________ invisible. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Are these sentences correct or incorrect? If they are incorrect, try to replace the adverb 
with a more appropriate one. More than one right answer is possible. 
1. It was an extremely horrible crime. 
2. This equipment is completely valuable. 
3. Our clothes were totally soaked after we got caught in a thunderstorm. 
4. The customer service at that store is perfectly awful. 
5. She has a very successful career as a consultant. 
6. I found the lecture nearly boring. 
7. The information is out of date, so it's slightly useless. 
8. Unfortunately our dishwasher is rather noisy. 
9. His suggestion was absolutely clever. 
10. I can't talk right now - I'm a bit busy. 
 
 
 
Writing Task 
Think of something you recommend – it could be: 
• a product 
• a place 
• an activity 
• a book or film 
Imagine you have been hired to write an advertisement or commercial for this thing. 
Use “exaggerated” and extreme adjectives to really emphasize its wonderful aspects 
and benefits. Send me your text at shayna@espressoenglish.net for feedback and 
correction! 
 
 


Answers – Quiz – Lesson 26 
Exercise 1: 
1. Your explanation was very clear; I understood everything perfectly. 
2. My neighbor drives a Ferrari. He's very rich. 
3. I was absolutely thrilled when I received the award. 
“completely” is also possible 
4. The renovation of the school is almost complete - there are only about two 
more weeks of work left. “practically” is also possible 
5. He responded to the situation in a very immature way. 
6. The whole experience was completely humiliating. 
“absolutely” is also possible 
7. The medicine has some very strong side effects. 
8. Until last year, the company's board of directors was entirely male. 
9. The unemployment rate is very high due to the global economic crisis. 
10. This hearing aid is so small that it's practically invisible. 
“almost” is also possible 
Exercise 2: 
1. Incorrect. Could be “absolutely” or “completely” horrible 
2. Incorrect. Could be “very” or “extremely” valuable 
3. Correct 
4. Correct 
5. Correct 
6. Incorrect. Could be “rather,” “somewhat,” or “fairly” boring 
7. Incorrect. Could be “completely” useless 
8. Correct 
9. Incorrect. Could be “very” or “extremely” clever 
10. Correct 


Answers – Quizzes in Lesson  
Which one is the extreme adjective? 
1. terrible 
2. spotless 
3. fascinating  
4. hilarious 
5. starving 
6. ancient 
7. exhausted 
8. astonishing 
Which one is the absolute adjective? 
1. unknown 
2. essential 
3. universal 
4. equal 
5. ideal 
Which one is the classifying adjective? 
1. an atomic weapon 
2. a pine tree 
3. a government worker  
4. a silk shirt 
5. an American tradition  
In which sentence can you insert the adverb? 
• His accent sounded slightly foreign. 
• We need to reform foreign policy. 
• Go away. This is private property. 
• He's a rather private person. 
• Is that an original painting or a reproduction? 
• That's a very original idea!
