lessons.title: Lesson 42
lessons.fullText:
Lesson 42: Reported Speech (Part 1) 
We use “reported speech” to talk about what somebody said in the past: 
 
• Direct Speech:  
Sally (yesterday): “I’m tired.” 
• Reported Speech:  
Sally said she was tired. 
• Direct Speech: 
John (last week): “I’ve finished my final exams.” 
• Reported Speech: 
John said he’d finished his final exams. 
 
This is one of the most complicated aspects of English, as there are many details to 
remember – so let’s get started! 
Verb Backshift 
The first rule of reported speech is that the main verb “backshifts” – it changes to 
another tense further in the past.  
In the examples above, the simple present (“I’m tired.”) changes to the simple past 
(“she was tired”) and the present perfect (“I’ve finished”) changes to the past 
perfect (“he’d finished”). 
Here’s how each tense changes: 
Direct Speech 
Reported Speech 
present simple 
 
“I’m hungry.” 
  past simple 
 
She said she was hungry. 
present continuous 
 
“We’re eating dinner.” 
 past continuous 
 
They said they were eating dinner. 


past simple 
 
“I saw the movie.” 
 
past perfect 
 
He said he’d seen the movie. 
 
He said he hadn’t called her yet. 
present perfect 
 
“I haven’t called her yet.” 
past continuous 
 
“I was thinking about taking a 
trip.” 
 
past perfect continuous 
 
She said she’d been thinking about 
taking a trip. 
can 
 
“I can’t hear you.” 
 
could 
 
He said he couldn’t hear me. 
will 
 
“My secretary will send the 
documents.” 
 
would 
 
She said her secretary would send the 
documents. 
 
NO backshift is necessary when the original verb is could, might, would, should, or 
in the past perfect: 
• Gary: “Could you help me?”  Gary asked if I could help him. 
• Nora: “I might quit my job.”  Nora said she might quit her job. 
• Jill: “I would love to visit China.”  Jill said she would love to visit China. 
• Bob: “I had never been so depressed.”   
Bob said he had never been so depressed. 
 
Reported Questions 
To talk about reported questions, we usually use the word asked or wanted to 
know. The tense of the main verb in reported questions follows the same 
“backshift” rules as in reported statements: 


• Jim: “Are you doing anything on Friday night?” 
Jim asked if I was doing anything on Friday night. 
Present continuous (are doing)  Past continuous (was doing) 
• Rachel: “Have you ever gone skiing?” 
Rachel asked if I had ever gone skiing. 
Present perfect (have gone)  Past perfect (had gone) 
• Nancy: “Where did you buy your computer?” 
Nancy wanted to know where I’d bought my computer. 
Simple past (did buy)  Past perfect (had bought) 
• Julia: “Can you read Russian? If so, will you help me translate this document?” 
Julia asked if I could read Russian and if I would help her translate a 
document. 
Can / will  Could / would 
• Steve: “How many kids do you have?” 
Steve asked me how many kids I had/have. 
No backshift needed because the situation (number of kids) continues to the 
present moment. We will learn more about special cases like this tomorrow. 
 
There are three main things to remember for reported questions: 
1. Do / Does / Did are NOT used in reported questions. 
 
“Where did you buy your computer?” 
She wanted to know where did I buy my computer. 
She wanted to know where I’d bought my computer. 
 
“How many kids do you have?” 
He asked me how many kids do I have. 
He asked me how many kids I have. 
 
“Does your mother like to travel?” 
They asked me does my mother like to travel. 
They asked me if my mother likes to travel. 
 


Including do/does/did is one of the most common errors when reporting questions. 
2.  In yes/no questions, use “if” or “whether” in the reported question. 
 
“Do you want anything to drink?” (answer: yes / no) 
The waitress asked if I wanted anything to drink. 
“Have you ever eaten sushi?” (answer: yes / no) 
Janine asked whether I’d ever eaten sushi. 
“Did you catch your flight?” (answer: yes / no) 
The travel agent wanted to know if I’d caught my flight. 
Again, notice that the auxiliary verbs “do” and “did” are not used in the reported 
question. 
3. In questions with the verb “to be,” the word order is subject + verb 
Notice the change in word order between the direct and reported question: 
“Is he from Mexico?” 
Tiffany asked if he was from Mexico. 
“Was she angry?” 
John asked if she was angry. 
“Are these your shoes?” 
Wanda asked if the white shoes were mine. 
“Were you born in Australia?” 
He wanted to know if I was born in Australia. 
Put it into practice! 
Say two questions someone recently asked you, and the two questions you recently 
asked someone else – using reported speech. For example: 
1. My husband asked me where the scissors were. 
(“Where are the scissors?”) 
 


2. I asked my teacher if there would be class on the weekend. 
(“Will there be class this weekend?”) 
 
 
Reported Requests & Commands 
Finally, we have reported requests (talking about asking someone to do something) 
and reported commands (talking about ordering someone do something more 
forcefully).  
These are fairly simple to report: 
• Use asked (person) to for requests. 
“Please make 10 copies of this report.” 
She asked me to make 10 copies of the report. 
• Use told (person) to for commands. 
“Stop bothering me.” 
He told me to stop bothering him. 
The main verb simply stays in the infinitive. Here are a couple more examples: 
• Request: “Chris, could you pass me the salt?” 
I asked Chris to pass me the salt. 
• Command: “Turn off the light when you leave.” 
I told her to turn off the light when she left. 
If you ask or tell somebody NOT to do something, we use these structures. We don’t 
include the word don’t in the reported request/command: 
• asked (person) not to 
“Please don’t use my real name in the article.” 
He asked the reporter not to use his real name in the article. 
• told (person) not to 
“Don’t touch the stove!” 
She told her son not to touch the stove. 
 
 


Summary 
• We use reported speech to talk about what somebody said in the past.  
• In reported speech, the main verb “backshifts” – it changes to another tense 
further in the past.  
• No backshift is necessary with should, could, would, might, or the past 
perfect. 
• To report questions, we use asked or wanted to know and backshift the 
main verb. Do not use do/does/did in reported questions. 
• When reporting yes/no questions, use if or whether.  
o "Do you understand?"  
o She asked if I understood. 
• When reporting questions with the verb "to be," the verb comes after the 
subject: 
o “Was she angry?” 
o John asked if she was angry. 
• To report requests, use asked (person) + to form of the verb.  
o She asked me to make 10 copies of the report. 
• For negative requests/commands, use asked/told (person) not to. Don't 
include the word "don't" in the reported speech.  
o My teacher told me not to use the word "don't" in reported speech. 
Tomorrow’s lesson will cover some exceptions and special cases involving reported 
speech – but for now, go ahead and take the quiz to review what you learned today! 
 
Writing Task 
Write about a recent conversation you had. What did you say? What did the other

Quiz – Lesson 42 
Exercise 1: Choose the right verb to complete each reported statement: 
1. Larry: “I’m going to buy some flowers for Anna.”

b) wasn’t / she’d just eaten

a) will/shall  
b) could/can

2 possible options: 
 
a) aren’t / weren’t  
 
b) haven’t been / hadn’t been

8. Lilly: “I was hoping you’d get the promotion.”

9. Melissa: “Bill and I got lost in Philadelphia.”

lessons.title: Lesson 43

Lesson 43: Reported Speech (Part 2) 
In yesterday’s lesson, you learned that in reported speech, the main verb 
“backshifts” – changes to a different tense further in the past. Today you’ll learn 
some exceptions to that rule, as well as a few other changes that may need to be 
made when reporting speech. 
No Backshift 
There are three cases in which you don’t need to backshift in reported speech. 
1) When talking about a general truth: 
• Teacher: “The earth revolves around the sun.” 
The teacher explained that the earth revolves around the sun. 
• Kevin: “The capital of the U.S. is Washington D.C.” 
Kevin said that the capital of the U.S. is Washington D.C. 
• Martha: “William Shakespeare died in the year 1616.” 
Martha pointed out that Shakespeare died in the year 1616. 
2) When talking about a situation that still continues to the present: 
In this case, the backshift is optional: 
• Linda: “I work in a bank.” 
Linda said she works in a bank. 
Linda said she worked in a bank. 
If Linda continues to work in a bank in the present, we can say either “works” or 
“worked” in the reported speech – both are correct. 
Here’s another example: 
• Mary: “My brother is taking English classes twice a week.” 
• Mary said her brother is / was taking English classes twice a week. 
If her brother continues to take English classes in the present, we can use “is” or 
“was” in the reported speech – both are correct. 
Now, if Mary’s brother has stopped attending English classes in the time since she 
made that statement, then we must backshift and add a phrase indicating that the 
situation existed only at the time that Mary made the statement in the past:  


• At the time, Mary said her brother was taking English classes twice a week.  
 
3) When reporting future statements that are still in the future: 
When we report on future statements, we must consider whether the event has now 
already passed, or whether it is still in the future. If it is still in the future, then the 
backshift is optional, but it is probably more common to just keep the verb the same: 
Direct 
Reported 
 
 
Sam: “I’ll lend you the money.” 
If Sam has not yet lent the money: 
Sam said he’ll/he’d lend me the money. 
If Sam has already lent the money:  
Sam said he’d lend me the money, and 
he gave it to me yesterday. 
 
 
Meredith: “I’m going on a date tonight.” 
 
If the date is still in the future: 
Meredith said she’s / she was going on 
a date tonight. 
If the date is now in the past: 
Meredith said she was going on a date 
that night. 
 
 
Changing Place & Time 
Sometimes we need to change other words in the reported speech as well, 
depending on place and time differences from the original statement. For example, 
let’s say Sally lives in Toronto, and her brother is visiting her: 
Direct 
Reported 
Sally: “My brother is here.” 
If we are currently in Toronto, we can 
say:  Sally said her brother is here. 
If we are NOT currently in Toronto, we 
must say: Sally said her brother is there. 
Sally said her brother is in Toronto. 


If we make the reported statement in the same place as the original statement, then 
there is no need to change “here” to “there” – but if we are in a different place, then 
we need to use “there” or else say the name of the place specifically: “in Toronto.” 
Here’s another example: 
Direct 
Reported 
Pedro (in a restaurant):  
“They have great salads here.” 
If we are in the same restaurant:  
Pedro said they have great salads here. 
If we are NOT in that restaurant:  
Pedro said they have great salads there. 
Pedro said they have great salads at the 
Olive Garden. 
 
A similar thing happens with “this” and “these,” because they are words used for 
something immediately visible or present with the speaker at that time. When 
reporting the speech, we need to specify the object: 
Direct 
Reported 
Sandra (looking at a dress in a store):  
“I love this dress!” 
Sandra said she loved the blue dress 
she saw in H&M. 
Jim (at the market):  
“These bananas are not yet ripe.” 
Jim said the bananas at the market 
were not yet ripe. 
 
Changes are also needed when the original statement contains a word related to 
time. For example, imagine that on Tuesday, Karen says, “We went to the zoo 
yesterday.” At that time, “yesterday” was Monday. 
However, if you’re speaking on Thursday, you can’t say “Karen said they’d gone to 
the zoo yesterday” – because on Thursday, “yesterday” = Wednesday.  
So we change “yesterday” to “the day before” or “the previous day.” Alternatively, 
we can specify the day: “Karen said they’d gone to the zoo on Monday.” 
Here’s a timeline showing this situation: 


Here are more examples of time changes that may be necessary when reporting: 
Direct speech 
Reported Speech 
now 
 
“I can’t talk now – I’m busy.” 
then / at that time / at the time 
 
He said he couldn’t talk at that time – he was 
busy. 
today 
 
“I’m looking after my 
neighbor’s kids today.” 
that day, on Monday 
 
She said she was looking after her neighbor’s kids 
that day. 
tonight 
 
(on Monday): “There’s no 
English class tonight.” 
that night, last night, on Monday night 
 
My classmate told me there was no English class 
on Monday night. 
tomorrow 
 
“We’re leaving for Italy 
tomorrow.” 
the next/following day, on Monday, today 
 
They said they were leaving for Italy the next 
day. 
yesterday 
 
“I spoke to her yesterday.” 
the day before/the previous day, on Monday 
 
John said he’d spoken to her the day before. 


last night 
 
 
“Ben drank too much last 
night.” 
the night before/the previous night, on 
Monday night 
 
Elena said Ben had drunk too much the previous 
night. 
this week 
 
“The conference is taking 
place this week.” 
that week, last week 
 
Pam said the conference was taking place that 
week. 
last month 
 
 
“The company made record 
sales last month.” 
the month before/the previous month, in May 
 
Joe reported that the company had made record 
sales in May. 
next year 
 
“I’m planning on going to 
college next year.” 
the following year 
 
Tim told me he was planning on going to college 
the following year. 
five minutes ago 
 
“Tara left the office five 
minutes ago.” 
five minutes before/five minutes earlier 
 
Fred explained that Tara had left the office five 
minutes earlier. 
 
Other words to use besides “said” 
Finally, remember that there are many other words you can use instead of “said” 
when reporting speech, such as mentioned, pointed out, told (someone), replied, 
responded, declared, stated, explained, added, and others. 
 
Summary 
• When talking about a general truth, no backshift is necessary: The teacher 
explained that the earth revolves around the sun. 
• When talking about situations that still exist, the backshift is optional, but it is 
often not used: Linda said she works/worked in a bank. 


• If the situation does NOT still exist, we must backshift and add a time phrase 
to make it clear that the situation was in the past, but not now. 
• When reporting future speech, the backshift is not necessary if the event is 
still in the future: He said he’ll lend me the money by Friday. 
• We may also need to modify place and time words like here, this, these, now, 
today, tonight, last night, ago, etc. 
• There are many synonyms for the word "said," which you can use when 
reporting speech. 
 
You’ve finished Lesson 43! Now take the quiz and try the writing task to continue 
practicing reported speech. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Quiz – Lesson 43 
Write these sentences in reported speech. If the backshift is not necessary, then don't 
backshift. Change any other words that may need to be changed. 
1. Brian: "The heater isn't working." (it has since been fixed) 
Brian complained that ___________________________________________________________ 
2. Tina (last week): "Mount McKinley is the highest peak in the U.S." 
Tina said that ____________________________________________________________ 
3. Isabel (yesterday): "The offices are currently closed for renovation, but they'll 
reopen next month." 
Isabel said that _____________________________________________________________ 
4. Phil (three days ago): "I have a headache. I'm going to lie down." 
Phil said _________________________________ and _____________________________________. 
5. Travis (last Monday): "We signed the agreement three days ago." 
Travis revealed that ____________________________________________________________. 
6. Rebecca (in the city center): "I come here every chance I get."  
(reporting from inside the city center): Rebecca said ________________________ 
_________________________________________________. 
7. Liz (yesterday): "I'm hoping to finish everything today." 
Liz told me ____________________________________________________________. 
8. Kent (last month): "My brother and I are running our own business now." 
(the business has since closed) 
Kent said that _________________________________________________________________. 
9. Mike (last Saturday): "I'll clean out the basement tomorrow." 
Mike said that ________________________________________________________________. 
10. Erin (a few minutes ago): "I'm going to a hockey game tomorrow." 
Erin told me that _____________________________________________________________. 


11. Christina (last year): "It won't be successful." (she was later proved wrong) 
Christina said that ______________________________________________________. 
12. Cory (in the park): "These bike paths aren't very well maintained."  
(reporting from outside the park): Cory said that ________________________________ 
____________________________________________________. 
 
 
Writing Task 
Describe a speech, an interview, or a scene from a movie that you remember well. 
Use reported speech to tell what each person said. Try to use at least a few of the 
alternatives to the word “said.” 
If you can’t remember a particular speech/interview/scene well enough, then look 
for a new one! You can go to YouTube and search for an interview with a well-
known person (example: “Steve Jobs interview”) – watch the video, then describe 
the person’s words in your writing task using reported speech.  
Ex) “When I hire somebody really senior, competence is the ante. They have to 
be really smart. But the real issue for me is, are they going to fall in love with 
Apple?” 
Steve Jobs said that the people he hired had to be really smart. He also 
considered whether or not they would fall in love with Apple. 
Send me your text at shayna@espressoenglish.net for feedback and correction! 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Answers – Quiz – Lesson 43 
Note: These are sample answers. Other correct answers might be possible. 
1. Brian complained that the heater wasn’t working. 
2. Tina said that Mount McKinley is the highest peak in the U.S. 
3. Isabel said that the offices are currently close for renovation, but they’ll 
reopen next month. 
4. Phil said he had a headache and he was going to lie down. 
5. Travis revealed that they had signed the agreement three days 
before/earlier.  
6.  (reporting from inside the city center): Rebecca said she comes here every 
chance she gets. 
7. Liz told me she was hoping to finish everything yesterday. 
8. (the business has since closed): Kent said that he and his brother were 
running their own business at the time. 
9. Mike said that he’d clean out the basement on Sunday. 
10. Erin told me that she’s going to a hockey game tomorrow. 
11. Christina said that it wouldn’t be successful. 
12. (reporting from outside the park): Cory said that the bike paths in the park 
aren’t very well maintained.

lessons.title: Lesson 44
lessons.fullText:
Lesson 44: Inversion & Cleft Sentences 
By now, you likely have a good grasp of the typical word order in English sentences. 
In today’s lesson, you’ll learn some ways we can alter the wording in a sentence to 
give particular emphasis to certain elements. 
Inversion 
You already know that in English, the word order is different in questions and 
statements. In statements, we but the subject before the auxiliary verb, and when 
asking a question, we put the auxiliary verb before the subject: 
• He doesn’t live in the city. 
Does he live in the city? 
• She can swim. 
Can she swim? 
• I’ve finished the work. 
Have you finished the work? 
• We should buy a new TV. 
Should we buy a new TV? 
 
However, there’s another situation in which we can “invert” the normal word order. 
Here are some examples of phrases that typically begin inverted sentences: 
• Never / Never before 
I had never felt so at peace. 
Never before had I felt so at peace. 
• Not only... but also 
I was late for the meeting and I spilled my coffee when rushing into the room. 
Not only was I late for the meeting, but I also spilled my coffee when rushing 
into the room. 
• Not until 
After I moved out, I understood how dysfunctional my family was. 
Not until I moved out did I understand how dysfunctional my family was. 
• No sooner 
Right after I cleaned the kitchen, my son spilled juice all over the floor. 
No sooner did I clean the kitchen than my son spilled juice all over the floor. 


• At no time 
The president was not aware of the corruption at any time. 
At no time was the president aware of the corruption. 
• Under no circumstances 
My sister and I weren’t allowed to stay out past 10 PM. 
Under no circumstances were my sister and I allowed to stay out past 10 
PM. 
• Rarely; seldom  
Pamela rarely offers to help. 
Rarely does Pamela offer to help. 
I have seldom felt so conflicted. 
Seldom have I felt so conflicted. 
• Only when; only after 
After he left the house, he realized he’d forgotten his wallet. 
Only after he left the house did he realize he’d forgotten his wallet. 
 
Notice that when there is no auxiliary verb in the original sentence, we actually ADD 
the auxiliary verb do or did in the inverted sentence: 
Pamela rarely offers to help  
 Rarely does Pamela offer to help. 
Right after I cleaned the kitchen…  
 No sooner did I clean the kitchen… 
When to use this structure? 
When you want to emphasize the negative expression at the beginning of the 
sentence. For example, when we compare: 
• I had never felt so at peace. 
• Never before had I felt so at peace. 
The first sentence focuses more on the feeling of peace, whereas the second 
sentence focuses more on the fact that I had NEVER had this feeling before. 
Here’s another example: 
• After I moved out, I understood how dysfunctional my family was. 


• Not until I moved out did I understand how dysfunctional my family was. 
The first sentence focuses more on the new understanding. The second sentence 
places more emphasis on the timing before arriving at this new understanding. 
The phrase “not only… but also…” functions to emphasize the second phrase as 
even better or worse than the first: 
• I was late for the meeting and I spilled my coffee when rushing into the 
room. 
In this sentence, both “being late” and “spilling the coffee” are treated as 
approximately equal 
• Not only was I late for the meeting, but I also spilled my coffee when 
rushing into the room. 
In this sentence, “being late for the meeting” is the less bad action, and “spilling 
my coffee” is the worse action – perhaps because it’s more embarrassing. 
 
You can also use “not only… but also…” for two good things, where the second one 
is better: 
• Not only did my husband make lunch, but he also washed the dishes 
without being asked! 
The latter action (washing dishes without being asked) are even better and 
more impressive than the first action (making lunch). 
Put it into practice! 
Think about when you experienced or realized something for the first time. Make a 
sentence with never before: 
• ________State the experience__________. Never before had I… 
Now think about a time when a situation went from good to great, or from bad to 
worse. Make a sentence with not only… but also: 
• Not only did ______________________, but ___________ also ___________________________. 
 


Cleft Sentences with It and What 
A “cleft sentence” is an alternative structure that can also be used to call attention 
to a specific part of the sentence. There are two main types of cleft sentences: 
1) Cleft Sentences beginning with IT 
 
Structure:  
• It + (form of verb “to be”) + subject + relative clause starting with that/who 
Examples: 
• A co-worker of mine first introduced me to meditation. 
 It was a co-worker of mine who first introduced me to meditation. 
• John received the promotion. 
 It was John who received the promotion. 
• I can’t stand the cold weather. 
 It’s the cold weather that I can’t stand. 
 
When to use this type of sentence? 
We often use it to shift the focus, such as when the other person is mistaken or is 
focusing on a different piece of information. For example: 
• “Religion is just a bunch of crazy ideas.” 
• “Actually, in Judaism it’s a person’s actions that matter most, not just their 
beliefs.” (shifts the focus from ideas to actions) 
 
• “How come you don’t like Canada? Is it a big culture shock?” 
• “No, it’s the cold weather that I can’t stand.” 
(shifts the focus from the culture to the weather) 
We can also use an it-cleft to distinguish one particular thing as standing out from 
the rest: 


• Although all of her books are famous, it is her first novel that remains on the 
bestseller list. 
2) Cleft Sentences beginning with WHAT 
 
Structure: 
What + less important part + form of the verb “to be” + [part to be emphasized] 
Normal:  
We really need a good night’s sleep. 
Cleft:   
What we really need is a good night’s sleep. 
Normal:  
I wanted to buy a poster. 
Cleft:   
What I wanted to buy was a poster. 
Normal: 
The music was great, but the dancers really amazed me. 
Cleft:  
The music was great, but what really amazed me were the dancers. 
Remember from our lesson on subject/verb agreement that in these types of 
sentences, we can use either was or were if the noun following it is plural. 
Similarly to the cleft sentences beginning with IT, we can use cleft sentences 
beginning with WHAT to shift the focus. Consider these examples: 
• “Glad you arrived safely! Are you hungry? Do you want to go out to eat?” 
• “No thanks. What we really need is a good night’s sleep.” 
(the cleft sentence changes the focus from eating to sleeping) 
 
• “What I wanted to buy was a poster, but I didn’t like any of the designs, so I 
got a T-shirt instead.” 
(the cleft sentence highlights the contrast between what I had intended to buy 
and what I actually bought) 
 
• “He has many good qualities, but what’s most impressive is his dedication.”  
(the cleft sentence calls special attention to his dedication among his many good 
qualities) 
We can also “invert” the order of the cleft sentence. There is no difference in 
meaning or emphasis; it’s just an alternative way to express it: 


• Regular sentence: He wanted money. 
• WHAT-cleft 1: What he wanted was money. 
• WHAT-cleft 2: Money was what he wanted. 
• IT-cleft: It was money that he wanted. 
There’s no particular reason to choose an IT-cleft or a WHAT-cleft, it just depends 
on which way you’d prefer to say the sentence. 
Summary 
• Inversion and cleft sentences are used to give special emphasis to a certain 
part of a sentence. 
• In inverted sentences, we put the auxiliary verb before the subject:  
o Never before had I felt so at peace.  
o Rarely does Pamela offer to help. 
• If there’s no auxiliary verb in the original sentence, we add do/does/did to 
the inverted sentence. 
• Inverted sentences often begin with never/never before, not only... but also, 
not until, no sooner, at no time, under no circumstances, rarely/seldom, only 
when, only after 
• We often use inverted sentences to emphasize the timing or circumstances. 
• Cleft sentences can begin with IT or WHAT: 
o It's the cold weather that I can't stand. 
o What we really need is a good night's sleep. 
• We often use cleft sentences to shift the focus and highlight one of the 
things/people in the sentence. 
You’ve finished Lesson 44! Now take the quiz for more practice with inverted 
sentences and cleft sentences. 
 
 
 
 
 


Quiz – Lesson 44 
Exercise 1: Rephrase the sentences into inverted sentences. 
1. Hate speech will not be tolerated under any circumstances. 
Under no circumstances _______________________________________________________. 
2. I only stopped worrying about my daughter after she called me. 
Only after _______________________________________________________________________. 
3. He rarely listened to advice. 
Rarely __________________________________________________________________________. 
4. We only discovered how difficult it was to bake bread when we tried it. 
Only when ____________________________________________________________________. 
5. We had never considered the possibility of being wrong. 
Never _________________________________________________________________________. 
6. Children may not be left unattended on the playground at any time. 
At no time ____________________________________________________________________. 
7. She has fifteen cats and she spends a fortune on taking care of them. 
Not only _______________________, but ________ also ___________________________________. 
8. We seldom learn from our mistakes. 
Seldom ______________________________________________________________. 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Exercise 2: Rewrite these sentences with IT or WHAT cleft sentences to emphasize the 
part in bold. 
Ex) I didn't invite them  It wasn't me who invited them. 
I like the diversity of the city.  What I like about the city is the diversity. 
1. Her attitude really annoyed me. (it) 
__________________________________________________________________________________ 
2. Sitting in this chair all day makes my back ache. (what) 
__________________________________________________________________________________ 
3. My sister can't carry a tune. (it) 
__________________________________________________________________________________ 
4. You should mind your own business. (what) 
__________________________________________________________________________________ 
5. The challenging acrobatics got me hooked on gymnastics. (it) 
__________________________________________________________________________________ 
6. Everyone told her she should give up. She doubled her efforts instead. 
(what) 
__________________________________________________________________________________ 
7. Most people don't know how poorly the factory workers are treated. 
(what) 
__________________________________________________________________________________ 
8. I'm an accountant, but I'm truly passionate about theater. (what) 
__________________________________________________________________________________ 
9. I helped out a bit, but my kids built the treehouse. (it) 
__________________________________________________________________________________ 
10. All the subjects are challenging, but all the students dread organic 
chemistry. (it) 
__________________________________________________________________________________ 


Writing Task 
Write about an important or significant event/experience in your life, which you 
have not yet written about during this course. Use at least three sentences with the 
structures we learned in this lesson: 
• Inversion, beginning with one of the expressions in the list 
• Cleft sentence beginning with “It” 
• Cleft sentence beginning with “What” 
Send me your text at shayna@espressoenglish.net for feedback and correction! 
 
 
Answers – Quiz – Lesson 44 
Exercise 1: 
1. Under no circumstances will hate speech be tolerated. 
2. Only after my daughter called me did I stop worrying about her. 
3. Rarely did he listen to advice. 
4. Only when we tried to bake bread did we discover how difficult it was. 
5. Never had we considered the possibility of being wrong. 
6. At no time may children be left unattended on the playground. 
7. Not only does she have fifteen cats, but she also spends a fortune on taking 
care of them. 
8. Seldom do we learn from our mistakes. 
 
 
 
 


Exercise 2: 
1. It was her attitude that really annoyed me. 
2. What makes my back ache is sitting in this chair all day. 
3. It’s my sister who can't carry a tune. 
4. What you should do is mind your own business.  
5. It was the challenging acrobatics that got me hooked on gymnastics.  
6. Everyone told her she should give up, but what she did instead was double 
her efforts.  
7. What most people don't know is how poorly the factory workers are treated.  
8. I'm an accountant, but what I'm truly passionate about is theater.  
9. I helped out a bit, but it was my kids who built the treehouse.  
10. All the subjects are challenging, but it’s organic chemistry that all the students 
dread.

Lesson 45 – Substitution & Elimination 
There are some situations in which we eliminate or substitute words in order to 
make the sentence shorter. Today's lesson will teach you some of these "shortcuts" 
in the English language. 
one / ones / some 
To avoid repeating a countable noun, we can use one or ones: 
• “Does anybody have a pen?” 
“Here's one you can use.” 
• All the paintings are nice, but my favorite is the one of the ocean. 
• I thought the silver earrings looked best on her, but she bought the gold ones. 
• “Can you pass me those headphones?” 
“These?” 
“No, the other ones - the ones with the microphone attached.” 
To substitute uncountable nouns, we can use some: 
• “I need more paper.” 
“Here's some you can use.” 
• There's fresh-squeezed orange juice in the fridge. Do you want some? 
When using ones, we must define exactly which things we are talking about. If we 
do not define which things specifically, then we use some even for countable nouns. 
Compare these sentences: 
• I ate most of the cookies, but I saved some for my brother. 
• I ate most of the cookies, but I saved the chocolate ones for my brother. 
• You forgot to water the flowers, and now some are dead. 
• You forgot to water the flowers, and now the ones near the window are 
dead. 
We also do not use one/ones... 
1) After nouns that are used as adjectives: 
• I thought he was on the soccer team, but he's actually on the basketball team. 
the basketball one. 
• We visited an art museum and a science museum. 
a science one. 


2) After possessives (instead, just use the possessive ending in -S): 
• My calculator is broken; can I use yours? 
yours = your calculator 
• After I cut my hair, my sister wanted to cut hers to match. 
hers = her hair 
The word one/ones is optional in the following situations: 
1) After which 
• I have three screwdrivers; I'm not sure which (one) is the size you need. 
• You've tried on ten pairs of jeans. Which (ones) do you like the best? 
2) After superlatives 
• I've caught a lot of fish, but this is the biggest (one) I've ever seen! 
• I'm going to teach you several things. I'll start with the most important 
(one). 
3) After either, neither, each, another 
• Two of the houses by the lake are for sale, but neither (one) is within our 
price range. 
• She frosted the cupcakes and placed a cherry on top of each (one). 
• After he finished the book, he read another (one) by the same author. 
so / not 
We can use the word so to substitute part of a sentence, so that we don't have to 
repeat it. This is usually used with verbs involving thinking. It can also be used with 
say and tell (someone): 
• “Do you think I'll get the job?” 
“I think so. You have all the right skills.” 
= I think you’ll get the job. 
• “Did you pass all your final exams?” 
“I hope so. I haven't gotten my grades yet.” 
= I hope I passed the exams. 
• He thought my idea was brilliant, and said so. 
= said that my idea was brilliant 


• “You’re telling me the flight has been canceled?!” 
“I’m afraid so.” 
= I regret to inform you that the flight has been canceled. 
We can use so after the following verbs: 
Can use “so” after: 
Cannot use “so” after: 
be afraid (in the sense of regret) 
appear/seem 
assume 
believe 
expect 
guess 
hope 
imagine 
suppose 
suspect 
think 
say 
tell (someone) 
accept 
admit 
agree 
be certain 
doubt 
hear 
know 
promise 
suggest 
be sure 
 
For example: 
• She'll help me out. She promised she would. 
She promised so. 
• Has he ever been arrested? I doubt it. / I doubt he has. 
I doubt so. 
In negative sentences, we have two ways of saying it: using not, and using not + 
verb + so: 
• “Is the store open on Sunday?” 
“I don't think so.” 
• “It looks like the store isn't open.” 
“I guess not.” 
We typically use not + verb + so with believe, expect, imagine, think. 
• “Is it going to rain tomorrow?” 
“I don’t believe so.” 
We typically use not with be afraid, guess, hope, suspect. 


• “It won’t be possible, will it?” 
“I’m afraid not.” 
• “Is it going to rain tomorrow?” 
“I hope not.” 
do so / to 
We can use do so (or does so, did so, doing so, etc.) as a substitute for a verb 
phrase: 
• I wanted to paint my nails, but I didn't have time to do so. 
• The students promised to clean up, but they left without doing so. 
• He asked me to make the phone call and I did so immediately. 
• They walk their dog every morning; they've done so for the past five years. 
We typically use these with action verbs, not state verbs. 
In conversational English, we sometimes end a phrase with "to" without including 
the verb when it is clear from the context what action we are talking about. 
• We wanted to travel this month, but we won't be able to. 
• "Are you going to have any more kids?" 
"We're not planning to." 
The only time we cannot end with "to" is if the verb that follows it is "be." Compare 
these sentences: 
• She made way more food than she needed to. 
• The meeting was way longer than it needed to be. 
• "Do you ever go horseback riding?" 
"When I was younger, I used to." 
• "Are you a technician?" 
"I used to be. Now I'm a supervisor." 
Conversational deletion 
Finally, in informal English, you will sometimes hear yes/no questions being asked 
without the auxiliary verb: 
• Is everyone ready?  Everyone ready? 
• Are you hungry?  You hungry? 
• Did he get married recently?  He get married recently? 
• Have you ever been to Mexico?  You ever been to Mexico? 


Sometimes, when the subject of the sentence is you, the question is asked without 
either the auxiliary verb or the subject: 
• Are you hungry?  Hungry? 
• Do you want to join us?  Wanna join us? 
• Do you ever find yourself daydreaming?  Ever find yourself daydreaming? 
• Have you been thinking about traveling?  Been thinking about traveling? 
This is not grammatically correct, but it does sometimes happen in informal English. 
I’m not advising you to speak this way – I just want you to be able to recognize it 
when you hear it! 
Summary 
• We can use one/ones to avoid repeating a countable noun. 
o 
Does anybody have a pen? I need one. 
o 
I ate most of the cookies, but I saved the chocolate ones for my 
brother. 
• We can use some to substitute uncountable nouns or non-specific plural 
countable nouns: 
o 
This soup is delicious. Do you want some? 
o 
I ate most of the cookies, but I saved some for my brother. 
• Don't use one/ones after nouns that are used as adjectives or after 
possessives. One/ones is optional after which, superlatives, either, 
neither, each, and another. 
• The word so can be used after some "thinking" verbs to substitute part of a 
sentence. 
o 
"Did you pass your exams?" 
o 
"I hope so." 
• To make the negative, we can do it in two ways: 
o 
I don't think so. 
o 
I hope not. 
• Use do so as a substitute for an action verb phrase.  
o 
I wanted to paint my nails, but I didn't have time to do so. 
• We sometimes end a phrase with "to" without including the verb when it is 
clear from the context what action we are talking about. The only exception is 
when the verb after it is "be." 
o 
She made way more food than she needed to. 
o 
The meeting was way longer than it needed to be. 


• In informal English, auxiliary verbs and the subject "you" are sometimes 
omitted from yes/no questions: Are you hungry?  You hungry? / Hungry?

Quiz – Lesson 45 
Exercise 1: Complete the sentences with one, ones, some, or nothing. 
1. He was still hungry after eating the sandwich, so I made him another 
__________. 
2. Most of the wine is domestic, but __________ is imported. 
3. They have three cats. The white __________ is the friendliest. 
4. We've run out of eggs. Could you buy __________ the next time you go to the 
store? 
5. She just bought a new bike and offered me her old __________. 
6. These trees are ancient - __________ are more than 500 years old. 
7. There are 16 songs on the CD, but this is the only __________ I like. 
8. I hate taking pills, especially the __________ that are large and hard to swallow. 
9. These two backpacks are very similar. Which __________ do you prefer? 
10. These aren't my keys. I must have grabbed the wrong __________.

Writing Task

your life, describe two "best practices" that you believe are good for education, and 
two "worst practices" that you believe are harmful to students' development. Try to 
use 2-3 of the structures from this lesson, where appropriate. Send me your text at

1. He was still hungry after eating the sandwich, so I made him another. 
2. Most of the wine is domestic, but some is imported. 
3. They have three cats. The white one is the friendliest.

5. She just bought a new bike and offered me her old one. 
6. These trees are ancient - some are more than 500 years old.

9. These two backpacks are very similar. Which do you prefer?
